note: Game research corpus (Stage 1). Produced by Codex from public knowledge of well-documented games, curated by Claude. Purpose: extract reusable mechanics, never copy titles.

games.title: Papers, Please
games.target_player: Players who enjoy close observation, rule application, time management, and morally difficult choices
games.goal: Process enough border entrants accurately to support the inspector's family while responding to changing laws, personal requests, and political events.
games.core_action: Compare documents, inspect personal details, identify discrepancies, question entrants, and decide whether to approve, deny, detain, or otherwise handle each case.
games.information: The player reads the current rulebook, official bulletins, passports, permits, identity details, dates, issuing locations, transcripts, and evidence revealed by inspection tools.
constraints: A workday has limited time.
Entry regulations change and accumulate.
Mistakes can produce citations and financial penalties.
The desk has limited space, so documents and tools must be organized.
The inspector's wages must cover food, heat, rent, medicine, and other family needs.
Moral requests may conflict with official rules and personal survival.
decisions: Which details should be checked first?
Is a mismatch a valid discrepancy or an innocent variation?
Should the entrant be questioned, searched, fingerprinted, detained, approved, or denied?
Should the player obey regulations or accept the cost of helping someone?
How should limited household income be allocated?
games.feedback: Stamps and border-gate animations show immediate decisions; citations identify errors; entrants react to the outcome; an end-of-day screen reports income, expenses, family status, and consequences.
games.failure: Errors reduce earnings, while slow work limits the number of paid cases. The family can become sick or die if its needs are neglected, and some choices can lead to arrest, death, or an unfavorable ending.
games.retry_motivation: Players want to improve inspection speed, avoid overlooked contradictions, protect the family, explore alternate moral choices, and discover different endings.
games.mastery: Skilled players internalize changing regulations, establish an efficient inspection order, organize the desk well, and recognize common discrepancies quickly. They also anticipate the financial and narrative consequences of bending a rule.
games.variation: Entrant documents, discrepancies, special encounters, changing regulations, scripted political events, and the player's moral choices vary the work and its consequences.
games.progression: New document types, rules, inspection tools, threats, and overlapping exceptions are introduced across successive workdays.
games.reward: Correct processing earns wages and citation-free streaks, while narrative revelations, family survival, tokens, and alternate endings reward careful or values-driven play.
games.core_loop_statement: Read the current rules, compare one person's evidence against them, investigate suspicious details, and issue a decision before time runs out. The thinking lives in spotting contradictions efficiently while deciding whether correctness, compassion, or survival matters most.
games.mastery_statement: A novice checks documents slowly and inconsistently. An expert uses a reliable scan order, remembers exceptions, and understands when a deliberate rule violation is worth its cost.
games.replay_statement: A new attempt can use a faster checking routine, different household priorities, or different responses to moral requests. These choices can reveal other consequences and endings.
games.kid_translation_note: Children could compare simple job requests with picture-based rules, such as choosing the right tools or safety gear for a task. Gentle dilemmas could ask them to balance rules, helpfulness, time, and team needs without severe consequences.

games.title: Overcooked
games.target_player: Friends, families, and groups who enjoy accessible controls, rapid coordination, and humorous teamwork
games.goal: Prepare, cook, assemble, and serve enough correct dishes before the timer expires to earn the required score.
games.core_action: Move around a kitchen, collect ingredients, chop or cook them, transfer items between stations, wash dishes, assemble orders, and deliver completed meals.
games.information: Players observe the order queue, recipe icons, timers, ingredient and appliance locations, cooking progress, dirty plates, hazards, teammate positions, and the kitchen's changing layout.
constraints: Each level has a time limit.
Orders must be completed accurately and preferably in queue order.
Ingredients require specific preparation steps.
Cooking food can burn if ignored.
Players have limited hands and must use shared stations.
Kitchen layouts create travel bottlenecks and may move or separate players.
decisions: Who should perform each role?
Which order or preparation step is most urgent?
Should work be specialized or reassigned as conditions change?
Where should ingredients and finished components be staged?
When should a player stop preparing food to wash dishes, prevent burning, or help a teammate?
games.feedback: Visible preparation states, cooking meters, alarms, fires, order completion, tips, score changes, character reactions, and a post-level star rating show performance.
games.failure: The team may miss the target score, lose tips through late or incorrect orders, waste time, burn food, or temporarily disrupt the kitchen. A failed level can be restarted without lasting punishment.
games.retry_motivation: Short levels make another attempt easy, and teams can immediately apply a better division of labor, cleaner communication, or more efficient route.
games.mastery: Skilled teams assign roles, communicate in short actionable phrases, build ingredient pipelines, stage future orders, avoid blocking one another, and adapt roles when the kitchen changes.
games.variation: Recipes, kitchen layouts, hazards, moving platforms, separated work areas, order sequences, team size, and human coordination create different situations.
games.progression: Later kitchens add recipes, longer process chains, tighter layouts, moving environments, hazards, and more demanding score thresholds.
games.reward: Points, tips, star ratings, unlocked levels, new chefs, and the satisfaction of smooth team coordination reinforce improvement.
games.core_loop_statement: Read incoming orders, divide a multi-step workflow among teammates, hand off materials, and serve finished products against the clock. The fun comes from turning confusion into a coordinated production line.
games.mastery_statement: Novices chase whichever task looks urgent and often duplicate work. Experts anticipate upcoming needs, maintain clear roles and staging areas, and recover quickly when the plan breaks.
games.replay_statement: Teams can retry with different roles, routes, station assignments, or communication rules. Even the same level changes because people coordinate differently each time.
games.kid_translation_note: A career game could turn a workplace into a simple shared process, such as receiving library books, preparing a school event, or helping at a bakery. Children would learn that jobs connect through handoffs and that clear teamwork matters.

games.title: Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney
games.genre: Narrative adventure and courtroom deduction game
games.target_player: Players who enjoy character-driven mysteries, reading, evidence comparison, and dramatic logical contradictions
games.goal: Investigate criminal cases and prove the defendant's innocence by exposing contradictions and identifying the true sequence of events.
games.core_action: Read dialogue, examine locations, gather evidence, question people, compare testimony with the court record, press suspicious statements, and present contradictory evidence.
games.information: The player reads witness testimony, character dialogue, evidence descriptions, photographs, diagrams, profiles, investigation observations, and revised statements.
constraints: Only collected evidence can usually be presented.
Evidence must be presented at the relevant testimony statement.
Incorrect courtroom choices reduce a penalty meter.
Some information is unavailable until the player examines or discusses the correct subject.
The story largely follows a prescribed sequence.
decisions: Which location, object, or person should be investigated next?
Which testimony statement deserves further pressure?
Does a statement conflict with evidence, timing, location, motive, or physical possibility?
Which evidence proves the contradiction?
Which explanation best connects the discovered facts?
games.feedback: New dialogue and evidence appear during investigation; courtroom objections trigger dramatic reactions, testimony revisions, judge responses, and story revelations. Mistakes visibly reduce the penalty meter.
games.failure: Too many incorrect courtroom answers can end the trial in a guilty verdict and require reloading or retrying. Most investigation errors cost time or produce corrective dialogue rather than permanent loss.
games.retry_motivation: Players want to resolve the mystery, protect the defendant, see dramatic character reactions, and experience the next revelation in the case.
games.mastery: Skilled players distinguish important wording from flavor text, maintain a coherent timeline, revisit evidence descriptions after new revelations, and present the precise proof at the precise statement.
games.variation: Cases introduce different characters, evidence sets, crimes, locations, testimony structures, twists, and deduction formats, although an individual case is mostly authored and fixed.
games.progression: Cases generally grow longer and more intricate, introducing larger evidence sets, layered testimony, hidden relationships, and contradictions that require combining several facts.
games.reward: Story revelations, overturned testimony, dramatic objections, cleared defendants, character development, and access to the next episode reward successful deduction.
games.core_loop_statement: Gather facts, listen to a claim, identify the exact part that cannot coexist with the evidence, and present proof. The thinking lives in converting a large story into a precise contradiction.
games.mastery_statement: A novice presents evidence based on a general suspicion. An expert tracks wording, time, place, and causality closely enough to identify exactly what is wrong and why.
games.replay_statement: The central solution is fixed, so replay variation is limited. Players can revisit cases to catch foreshadowing, test optional dialogue, or solve contradictions with fewer mistakes.
games.kid_translation_note: Children could interview friendly workers, collect picture clues, and correct harmless misunderstandings about how a job is done. The emphasis should be on explaining evidence clearly rather than accusing characters.

games.title: Mini Metro
games.genre: Real-time transit-network strategy and puzzle game
games.target_player: Players who enjoy minimalist systems, spatial planning, optimization, and gradually escalating pressure
games.goal: Keep a growing city's passengers moving by designing an efficient rail network and prevent any station from remaining overcrowded for too long.
games.core_action: Draw and redraw rail lines between stations, assign trains and carriages, place tunnels or bridges, and reorganize the network as demand grows.
games.information: Players observe station shapes, passenger destination shapes, waiting crowds, line colors, train positions, route topology, river crossings, congestion warnings, and available resources.
constraints: The number of lines, trains, carriages, tunnels, or bridges is limited.
Trains have limited capacity.
Passengers require access to stations matching their destination symbols.
Rivers and geography restrict connections.
Stations and demand continue appearing over time.
A persistently overcrowded station ends the run in the standard mode.
decisions: Which stations should share a line?
Where should lines intersect to support transfers?
Should a route be extended, split, looped, or completely redrawn?
Which congestion point deserves the next train or carriage?
Which weekly resource upgrade will best address future demand?
games.feedback: Passengers visibly queue, board, transfer, and reach destinations; trains animate along the network; overcrowding indicators escalate; statistics and a final passenger count summarize performance.
games.failure: A run ends when a station remains overcrowded beyond its warning period. The cost is the loss of that run, followed by a final score that can guide the next attempt.
games.retry_motivation: Players can immediately redesign their opening network, try a different upgrade, pursue a higher passenger count, or adapt better to a new station layout.
games.mastery: Skilled players create balanced routes, limit unnecessary line crossings, provide good access to rare station shapes, anticipate transfer loads, and rebuild proactively instead of waiting for total congestion.
games.variation: Station placement, station types, passenger demand, resource choices, city maps, geography, and growth order vary between runs.
games.progression: Within a run, stations and passengers accumulate while the player periodically receives limited new resources. Across maps, different geography and special rules create new planning problems.
games.reward: Higher passenger totals, longer survival, efficiency statistics, achievements, leaderboard performance, unlocked maps, and the visual elegance of a well-running network reinforce play.
games.core_loop_statement: Connect demand points, watch people move through the network, identify emerging congestion, and redesign or reinforce the weakest route. The fun lives in making a simple diagram absorb continuously growing complexity.
games.mastery_statement: A novice connects every new point to the nearest line. An expert considers network-wide capacity, transfer behavior, rare destinations, and future expansion before drawing a connection.
games.replay_statement: The next run can test different line shapes, transfer hubs, upgrade priorities, and responses to random growth. There is rarely one permanently correct network.
games.kid_translation_note: Children could connect people, tools, and workplaces with simple routes, then observe where help gets delayed. This can illustrate how transport, communication, and support jobs keep a community functioning.

games.title: SimCity
games.target_player: Players who enjoy open-ended planning, resource management, experimentation, and observing interconnected systems
games.goal: Build and sustain a functioning city by balancing growth, public services, infrastructure, finances, and citizen needs.
games.core_action: Zone land, construct infrastructure and services, set policies or budgets, inspect data, respond to problems, and revise the city plan as it grows.
games.information: Players read maps, demand indicators, budgets, population statistics, advisor messages, citizen feedback, traffic patterns, service coverage, land value, pollution, crime, and other system overlays.
constraints: Construction and services cost money.
Tax revenue depends on a functioning population and economy.
Land, terrain, and infrastructure placement limit expansion.
Residents and businesses require transportation and essential services.
Policies can create tradeoffs between growth, cost, health, safety, and satisfaction.
Different entries in the series simulate these systems differently.
decisions: Where should residential, commercial, and industrial areas be placed?
When should the city expand rather than improve existing districts?
Which service or infrastructure problem is most urgent?
How should taxes and service budgets be balanced?
Should an inefficient neighborhood be repaired incrementally or redesigned?
How much resilience should be built before a disaster or growth surge?
games.feedback: Buildings develop or decline, traffic and citizens move through the city, maps visualize system conditions, messages report needs, and financial and population statistics reveal longer-term effects.
games.failure: There is often no single mandatory loss state; a city can enter debt, lose population, suffer service collapse, or become difficult to recover. Some versions or scenarios impose explicit objectives, deadlines, or failure conditions.
games.retry_motivation: Players retry to build a more efficient or attractive city, test a different layout or policy, recover from earlier planning mistakes, complete scenarios, or explore emergent outcomes.
games.mastery: Skilled players interpret data overlays, anticipate infrastructure demand, preserve future expansion space, understand interacting systems, and solve underlying causes instead of treating visible symptoms.
games.variation: Maps, terrain, starting resources, disasters, growth patterns, player layouts, policies, scenarios, and simulation interactions produce different cities.
games.progression: The city grows from basic zoning and infrastructure into a larger system requiring transportation, utilities, specialized services, budget control, and regional planning. Exact unlock structures vary by series entry.
games.reward: Population growth, tax income, upgraded buildings, unlocked infrastructure, completed scenarios, positive city indicators, and the visible transformation of an empty map reinforce planning.
games.core_loop_statement: Build or zone an area, observe how people and systems respond, diagnose shortages or side effects, and invest in the next adjustment. The thinking lives in understanding that every local choice participates in a larger system.
games.mastery_statement: A novice reacts to each complaint separately and expands quickly. An expert reads trends, plans capacity and land use ahead of demand, and recognizes the shared cause behind several problems.
games.replay_statement: A new city can emphasize different layouts, industries, transport systems, budgets, or aesthetic goals. Changing one early planning assumption can produce a very different urban system.
games.kid_translation_note: A simplified town could let children place workplaces and public services, then see how each profession supports others. Clear visual links could show, for example, how drivers, nurses, builders, shopkeepers, and sanitation workers affect daily life.

games.title: Tetris
games.target_player: A broad audience seeking immediately understandable controls, spatial reasoning, escalating speed, and score mastery
games.goal: Arrange falling tetrominoes to complete horizontal lines, clear space, and survive while earning as many points as possible.
games.core_action: Move and rotate each falling piece, choose its landing position, and place it to complete lines or prepare the board for future pieces.
games.information: Players observe the current piece, the existing stack, empty-space shapes, landing position, cleared lines, score or level, and usually a preview of upcoming pieces; exact interface features vary by version.
constraints: Pieces use fixed geometric shapes.
Placed blocks generally cannot be moved individually afterward.
A piece must land within the board.
Incomplete rows remain and consume vertical space.
The fall speed increases in many versions.
Reaching the top ends the game.
decisions: Where should the current piece land?
Which rotation preserves a clean surface?
Should the player clear lines immediately or prepare a larger clear?
How much risk should be accepted to create a high-value setup?
How should an awkward piece be placed without creating an inaccessible hole?
games.feedback: Pieces lock into place, completed lines disappear, the stack drops, sound and animation celebrate clears, and score, level, speed, and game-over displays show performance.
games.failure: The game ends when new pieces can no longer enter or be placed because the stack has reached the top. The player loses the current run but can restart immediately.
games.retry_motivation: Restarts are nearly instant, personal errors are easy to recognize, and players can chase a higher score, longer survival, cleaner play, or advanced line-clear techniques.
games.mastery: Skilled players maintain a flat, flexible surface, avoid holes and overhangs, use previews to plan ahead, manage risk, place pieces rapidly, and intentionally construct high-scoring clears.
games.variation: Piece order, player placement choices, speed, modes, scoring rules, and optional modern features such as hold or ghost pieces vary by version and session.
games.progression: Difficulty primarily rises through increasing fall speed and stack pressure. Some versions also add goals, stages, opponents, modifiers, or alternative modes.
games.reward: Line clears, score increases, level advancement, audiovisual effects, high-score records, and the satisfaction of restoring order reinforce the loop.
games.core_loop_statement: Read the board and incoming shape, choose a rotation and landing place, then manage the new space created by that irreversible decision. The fun lies in continually turning an imperfect sequence into an orderly, flexible structure.
games.mastery_statement: A novice places pieces where they fit immediately. An expert protects future options, plans from previews, avoids structural holes, and deliberately balances safety against scoring opportunities.
games.replay_statement: Every sequence invites a different arrangement, and the player can retry with cleaner placements or a more ambitious scoring strategy. Small improvements are immediately visible.
games.kid_translation_note: Children could fit tasks, tools, or schedules into limited spaces while keeping future choices open. This could teach planning and organization through quick, low-reading interactions.

games.title: Slay the Spire
games.target_player: Players who enjoy turn-based tactics, probability, build construction, and repeated runs with consequential choices
games.goal: Climb a branching series of encounters, improve a deck and relic collection, defeat bosses, and ultimately complete the Spire's final challenge.
games.core_action: Draw cards, spend limited energy to play attacks, defenses, and powers, read enemy intentions, and choose rewards and routes that shape the deck for later battles.
games.information: Players observe their hand, draw and discard piles, energy, health, status effects, enemy intents, enemy health, relics, potions, map branches, card rewards, and upcoming encounter types.
constraints: Only drawn cards are available each turn.
Energy limits how many cards can be played.
Health persists between most encounters.
Deck additions affect the probability of drawing every other card.
Routes force tradeoffs among fights, elites, shops, rest sites, and unknown events.
Most run-specific cards and relics are lost when the run ends.
decisions: Which cards should be played and in what order?
How much damage should be blocked versus accepted?
Should a card reward be taken or skipped?
Which cards should be upgraded, removed, or purchased?
Which route offers the right balance of danger and improvement?
Does a reward strengthen the deck's actual plan or merely look powerful alone?
games.feedback: Damage, block, status effects, enemy intent changes, card animations, and combat previews show immediate results. Rewards, map progress, boss victories, unlocks, and run summaries show longer-term outcomes.
games.failure: If health reaches zero, the run ends and most run-specific progress is lost. The player retains knowledge and may retain or unlock broader progression such as cards, relics, characters, or increased challenge levels.
games.retry_motivation: Runs offer new card and relic combinations, branching routes, better strategic choices, unlocks, character play styles, and the possibility of overcoming a previously failed encounter.
games.mastery: Skilled players build coherent, compact decks, evaluate rewards relative to the current build, predict draw cycles, use enemy intents efficiently, preserve health, and choose routes based on whether the deck can handle their risks.
games.variation: Card rewards, relics, potions, enemies, events, shops, map paths, bosses, character selection, and difficulty modifiers create different runs.
games.progression: A run advances through acts with stronger enemies and bosses while the deck accumulates cards, upgrades, removals, and relic synergies. Across runs, unlocks and escalating difficulty levels deepen the challenge.
games.reward: New cards and relics, stronger synergies, gold, upgrades, boss rewards, unlocks, victories, and the discovery of unexpectedly powerful combinations reinforce experimentation.
games.core_loop_statement: Read enemy intent, assemble the best turn from a limited hand, then choose rewards and routes that reshape future possibilities. The deepest thinking lies in balancing immediate survival with construction of a coherent long-term strategy.
games.mastery_statement: A novice collects individually strong cards and reacts one turn at a time. An expert values consistency, synergy, draw probability, future encounters, and the option to reject a reward.
games.replay_statement: The next run can pursue another character, route, deck concept, or risk level, but random rewards may force the plan to evolve. Failure teaches which threats a future build must answer.
games.kid_translation_note: Children could assemble a small set of career skills, tools, and helpers, then choose how to solve visible workplace challenges. Rewards should encourage coherent combinations, such as listening plus note-taking plus teamwork, rather than simply collecting everything.

games.title: Return of the Obra Dinn
games.target_player: Players who enjoy careful observation, identity puzzles, timeline reconstruction, and making inferences from incomplete evidence
games.goal: Determine the identities and fates of the people aboard the Obra Dinn and reconstruct what happened during the ship's missing voyage.
games.core_action: Explore the ship, enter frozen scenes of death, inspect spatial and visual details, listen to final moments, connect people across scenes, and record identities and fates in a logbook.
games.information: Players study frozen three-dimensional scenes, short audio exchanges, voices and accents, clothing, uniforms, relationships, ship locations, crew manifests, illustrations, role labels, objects, causes of death, and who appears together.
constraints: Scenes show only a frozen moment and a short preceding audio fragment.
Important evidence may be indirect or located away from the central event.
Many people initially appear as unidentified faces.
Identity and fate entries require specific combinations from the logbook.
The game generally confirms deductions only in batches, limiting brute-force certainty.
Some conclusions depend on combining evidence from widely separated scenes.
decisions: Which scene, person, object, or background detail should be inspected?
Which faces across different memories represent the same person?
What does clothing, location, language, or social grouping imply about identity?
What precise fate occurred, and who or what caused it?
Which deductions are certain enough to enter before seeking more evidence?
games.feedback: The logbook fills with scenes, faces, locations, and written fate entries; correctly completed sets are formally confirmed and locked in; music and visual transitions mark discoveries and validation.
games.failure: There is little conventional failure and no combat loss. Incorrect deductions remain unconfirmed, costing time and potentially misleading later reasoning, while the player can continue revising entries.
games.retry_motivation: Players persist to resolve remaining identities, validate a theory, understand the complete tragedy, and experience the satisfaction of turning obscure clues into certainty.
games.mastery: Skilled players inspect the entire scene rather than only the corpse, track recurring groups and duties, distinguish direct evidence from inference, cross-reference distant memories, and manage confidence without relying on brute force.
games.variation: The authored mystery and its solution are fixed, but players can discover scenes, form hypotheses, and solve identities in different orders.
games.progression: New memories expose connected deaths and open further areas of the ship. Early direct clues establish the cast, while later deductions increasingly depend on cross-referencing occupations, relationships, language, location, and chronology.
games.reward: Confirmed deduction sets, newly accessible memories, completed logbook pages, narrative understanding, and the final evaluation of the investigation reward careful reasoning.
games.core_loop_statement: Enter a frozen event, search its foreground and background for clues, connect those observations to other moments, and record a hypothesis about identity and fate. The fun lives in extracting reliable conclusions from small, distributed details.
games.mastery_statement: A novice focuses on the obvious dramatic event. An expert studies roles, clothing, location, language, social groups, and recurring background figures, then separates proven facts from tentative inference.
games.replay_statement: The mystery itself does not change, so mechanical replay variation is limited. A replay can follow a different discovery order, solve with fewer speculative entries, or reveal foreshadowing that only makes sense after knowing the full story.
games.kid_translation_note: Children could explore frozen scenes from ordinary workplaces and infer who performs each role from tools, clothing, location, and teamwork. The mystery can focus on reconstructing how a successful project happened rather than investigating death.

games.title: Stardew Valley
games.genre: Farming and life-management simulation with role-playing elements
games.target_player: Players who enjoy relaxed planning, customization, relationships, collecting, and gradual growth
games.goal: Build a thriving farm and satisfying town life by choosing personal goals such as earning money, restoring the Community Center, developing relationships, exploring, and completing collections.
games.core_action: Repeatedly inspect the farm and town, choose how to spend the day, perform short actions such as planting, watering, harvesting, fishing, mining, crafting, shopping, and talking, then convert the results into money, materials, relationships, or progress.
games.information: The player observes the time, date, season, weather forecast, energy and health, crop growth, available money and materials, tool capabilities, shop offerings, requests, relationship levels, map locations, and predictable schedules or preferences learned over time.
constraints: Each day has limited time.
Most physical actions consume energy.
Crops grow only in appropriate seasons unless protected by special facilities.
Money, seeds, materials, inventory space, and tool quality limit available plans.
Characters, shops, fish, festivals, and resources may be available only at particular times, locations, seasons, or weather conditions.
Travel between activities consumes part of the day.
decisions: Which activities deserve today's limited time and energy
Whether to invest money in seeds, animals, tools, buildings, inventory, or other upgrades
Which crops to grow and whether to sell, process, store, gift, cook, or donate the output
Whether to pursue income, relationships, exploration, collections, or long-term restoration goals
How much risk and inventory space to commit to a mining trip
How to arrange and automate the farm
games.feedback: Actions produce immediate sounds, animations, item drops, energy changes, dialogue reactions, and visible task completion. Crops and buildings visibly develop over days, sales are summarized overnight, relationships gain hearts, skills level up, and collections or restoration projects fill in.
games.failure: There is usually no permanent game-over state. Running out of health or staying out too late can end the day and may cost money or items; neglected seasonal crops can die, and poor planning can waste time, energy, or investment. Most losses can be recovered through additional days of play.
games.retry_motivation: A failed or inefficient day reveals schedules, resource requirements, and better routines. Persistent farm growth, unfinished projects, upcoming seasons, character stories, and the possibility of a more efficient plan encourage another day.
games.mastery: Skilled players coordinate seasonal calendars, processing chains, character schedules, weather, travel routes, tool upgrades, and energy restoration. They turn early investments into automation and high-value production while pursuing several goals in the same trip.
games.variation: Seasons, weather, daily luck, resource drops, mine layouts, requests, festivals, chosen farm layout, crop strategy, relationships, specialization choices, and self-selected goals change the experience.
games.progression: New seasons introduce different crops, fish, events, and planning problems. Skill levels, tool upgrades, buildings, crafting recipes, relationships, deeper mine floors, restored locations, and story milestones gradually expand the player's options and production scale.
games.reward: Money, harvests, new items, upgraded tools, recipes, buildings, automated systems, relationship scenes, collection completion, restored spaces, visual farm improvement, and the satisfaction of executing a planned day reinforce the loop.
games.core_loop_statement: Read the day's conditions, choose a small set of priorities, perform work, and convert the results into future capability before time and energy run out. The thinking lives in balancing attractive short-term activities against investments that make later days easier or more valuable.
games.mastery_statement: A novice reacts to nearby tasks and frequently runs out of time or energy. An expert plans around calendars and routes, bundles compatible errands together, and builds systems that reduce repetitive work.
games.replay_statement: Next time, the player can choose a different farm layout, income strategy, relationship focus, upgrade order, or daily route. Even within one save, every new day supports a revised plan based on what the previous day taught.
games.kid_translation_note: A career game could give children a short workday, several useful tasks, and a visible workplace that improves through their choices. Simple calendars and limited energy can teach prioritization without making mistakes permanently punishing.

games.title: Pokémon Red/Blue
games.genre: Creature-collection role-playing game with turn-based battles
games.target_player: Children and general audiences who enjoy collecting, exploration, tactical battles, discovery, and creature growth
games.goal: Explore the region, catch and train a varied team, earn eight Gym Badges, defeat the Pokémon League, and optionally complete the Pokédex.
games.core_action: Explore routes and dungeons, encounter creatures or trainers, read battle conditions, choose a move, item, switch, or escape, then use the outcome to strengthen or revise the team.
games.information: The player reads creature species, level, current HP, status conditions, known moves, move type, remaining PP, opponent identity, battle messages, inventory, party order, terrain obstacles, NPC hints, and knowledge accumulated about type matchups and encounter locations.
constraints: The active party holds at most six Pokémon.
Each Pokémon can know at most four moves.
Moves have limited PP between restorations.
HP and status persist between many battles until healed.
Catching requires Poké Balls and is easier after weakening or inflicting status on the target.
Badge and field-move requirements gate parts of the world.
Items and money are limited, especially early in the journey.
Some Pokémon are exclusive to one version or normally require trading to obtain.
decisions: Which species and roles to include in the six-member party
Whether to attack, use a status or setup move, switch, use an item, or attempt escape
Which four moves each Pokémon should retain
Whether to catch, train, evolve, store, or replace a creature
How to balance team training instead of relying on one highly leveled creature
When to spend consumable items or return to a healing location
Which routes and optional areas to explore
games.feedback: Battles show HP changes, animations, sound effects, effectiveness messages, status effects, experience gains, level-ups, stat increases, evolution, and victory rewards. The Pokédex records discoveries, badges mark major progress, and newly learned field abilities open previously blocked paths.
games.failure: If every party member faints, the player blacks out, loses a portion of carried money, and returns to the most recent healing location. Battle and travel progress since the last save can also be lost if the player reloads, but trained creatures and collected resources otherwise persist after a blackout.
games.retry_motivation: The player can train, change the party, revise moves, buy supplies, study type matchups, or approach with a different lead. Near victories clearly suggest that one more level or a better tactical choice could succeed.
games.mastery: Skilled players anticipate opposing types and moves, preserve favorable matchups through switching, use status and stat-changing moves deliberately, manage PP and items across long routes, and construct a team with complementary strengths rather than selecting only by level.
games.variation: Wild encounters, capture success, critical hits, damage ranges, status effects, move accuracy, chosen starter, team composition, learned moves, evolution timing, route order, and version-exclusive species create different journeys.
games.progression: Routes introduce stronger and more varied opponents, while badges, field moves, and key items unlock new areas. Captures, experience, levels, evolutions, and new moves steadily increase team capability before the final sequence of elite battles.
games.reward: New creatures, Pokédex entries, experience, levels, moves, evolutions, money, items, badges, opened routes, memorable team attachment, and victories produced by a well-built team reinforce play.
games.core_loop_statement: Explore, encounter a challenge, choose actions from a compact battle menu, and turn victories or captures into a stronger and more flexible team. The thinking lives in matching capabilities to opponents while deciding which creatures deserve limited team space and training.
games.mastery_statement: A novice mainly uses the strongest-looking attack and favors the highest-level creature. An expert predicts matchups, switches proactively, values support moves, and develops a balanced team whose members cover one another's weaknesses.
games.replay_statement: A new journey can use a different starter, party, move set, evolution plan, or training balance. Individual defeats also invite an immediate experiment with another lead, matchup, or item strategy.
games.kid_translation_note: Career roles could become a small team of workers with different strengths, letting children match the right skill to each job. Growth should make familiar teammates visibly more capable while encouraging a balanced team rather than one universally best choice.

games.title: Zoombinis
games.target_player: Children developing logical reasoning, pattern recognition, hypothesis testing, and problem-solving skills
games.goal: Guide groups of Zoombinis through a sequence of logic puzzles to reach the safe settlement of Zoombiniville.
games.core_action: Observe a puzzle's reactions, compare Zoombini attributes, infer the hidden rule, then place or route each character according to the current hypothesis.
games.information: The player observes combinations of visible attributes such as hair, eyes, noses, and feet; puzzle layouts; environmental clues; accepted and rejected attempts; limited attempt indicators; and patterns connecting a character's features to successful destinations or arrangements.
constraints: Each traveling group contains a limited number of individually featured Zoombinis.
Puzzle rules must often be inferred from examples rather than stated directly.
Many puzzles allow only a limited number of incorrect attempts.
A wrong assignment may prevent one or more Zoombinis from continuing through that puzzle.
Later difficulty levels use more attributes, categories, exceptions, or interacting rules.
The player may need to continue with a smaller group after mistakes.
decisions: Which Zoombini to test first to gain the most useful information
Which visible attributes are relevant to the hidden rule
How to classify, order, pair, or route the group
Whether the evidence supports the current hypothesis
When to use a remaining mistake allowance on an uncertain test
How to revise the rule after a rejection
games.feedback: Puzzle characters and machines visibly accept or reject choices through expressive animations, sounds, and reactions. Successful Zoombinis move onward, mistakes consume opportunities or leave travelers behind, and arrival at camps or Zoombiniville makes rescued population progress visible.
games.failure: Incorrect choices can exhaust a puzzle's allowed mistakes and cause affected Zoombinis to be turned back or left unable to continue with the current group. The broader rescue campaign continues, so the player can bring later groups and use improved reasoning rather than facing a conventional game over.
games.retry_motivation: Every rejection is evidence about the hidden rule, making the next attempt better informed. Attachment to the distinctive characters, the desire to bring everyone safely home, and access to another group encourage renewed attempts.
games.mastery: Skilled players choose highly informative tests, isolate one variable at a time, track both positive and negative evidence, and infer general rules before committing the whole group. They minimize guesses and can explain why each placement should work.
games.variation: Zoombini feature combinations, group composition, puzzle instances, hidden mappings, chosen journey routes, surviving group size, and escalating puzzle difficulty vary the reasoning problem.
games.progression: The journey chains different kinds of logic problems together, and repeated journeys raise puzzle difficulty. Advanced versions demand classification across more features, multi-step deduction, tighter error management, and more complex relationships.
games.reward: Safe passage, expressive character celebrations, a growing Zoombiniville population, access to later journey sections, successful rule discovery, and the intrinsic satisfaction of a complete logical explanation reinforce play.
games.core_loop_statement: Observe attributes, test a classification or route, interpret acceptance or rejection, and refine the hidden rule until the group passes. The fun lives in converting playful reactions into evidence and reaching certainty with as few risky guesses as possible.
games.mastery_statement: A novice guesses from superficial resemblance and changes theories inconsistently. An expert designs informative tests, controls variables, remembers rejected cases, and applies a discovered rule to the entire group.
games.replay_statement: The next group presents different feature combinations and may expose weaknesses in the player's previous rule-finding method. A player can retry by testing a more diagnostic character first or by tracking evidence more systematically.
games.kid_translation_note: A career game could ask children to assign customers, tools, or materials by discovering a workplace rule from reactions. Friendly feedback can make mistakes useful clues, teaching that careful observation is part of real work.

games.title: Cooking Mama
games.genre: Cooking-themed collection of timing, motion, and dexterity minigames
games.target_player: Children, families, and casual players who enjoy short tactile challenges, recognizable food preparation, and score improvement
games.goal: Complete recipes by succeeding at a sequence of preparation and cooking minigames, earning strong evaluations and unlocking or completing more dishes.
games.core_action: Read a brief visual instruction, then repeatedly perform a short timed input such as chopping, stirring, peeling, pouring, shaping, controlling heat, or flipping food with the required rhythm and precision.
games.information: The player observes gesture demonstrations, tool and ingredient positions, timers, progress indicators, target shapes or quantities, color and cooking-state changes, warning cues, and Mama's immediate reactions.
constraints: Most recipe steps have strict time limits.
Inputs must follow the demonstrated direction, rhythm, order, or target area.
Overcooking, undercooking, spilling, inaccurate cutting, or missed timing lowers performance.
A recipe combines several different minigames, so one weak step can reduce the final evaluation.
The control scheme limits each task to a small set of gestures or button actions.
decisions: How quickly to work without losing accuracy
When to stop heating, pouring, stirring, or cutting
How to adjust motion after visual or audio warnings
Whether to prioritize clean precision or rapid completion when time is short
Which recipe to practice or attempt next
games.feedback: Ingredients visibly transform and tools respond directly to input. Timers, progress meters, success effects, mistakes, Mama's expressions and comments, per-step results, and a final recipe evaluation show performance.
games.failure: A poorly performed step produces a low evaluation or an imperfect dish rather than usually ending the entire game. The player generally continues to later steps and can replay the recipe to improve the result.
games.retry_motivation: Challenges are brief, mistakes are easy to identify, and better timing can quickly produce a higher rating. The humor of imperfect outcomes, Mama's reactions, recipe completion, and the desire to master every step support replay.
games.mastery: Skilled players recognize each minigame's cue-to-action pattern, use controlled and efficient motions, anticipate state changes instead of reacting late, and maintain accuracy under the timer across the full recipe.
games.variation: Recipes use different ingredient transformations, tools, gestures, timing windows, action sequences, and combinations of minigames. Performance variation also comes from the player's speed and precision.
games.progression: New recipes introduce different actions and more demanding combinations of familiar gestures. Improvement comes both from accessing more content and from learning the timing and control language shared by multiple recipe steps.
games.reward: Completed dishes, scores or evaluations, positive character reactions, unlocked recipes or content, visual food transformations, and immediate improvement over a previous attempt reinforce the loop.
games.core_loop_statement: Watch a tiny demonstration, perform one tactile job under time pressure, receive an immediate evaluation, and continue to the next step until the product is complete. The fun lives in turning recognizable work motions into short precision challenges and seeing raw ingredients transform.
games.mastery_statement: A novice reacts late, moves too broadly, or rushes and makes messy inputs. An expert anticipates cues, uses compact controlled motions, and balances speed with accuracy across every step.
games.replay_statement: The player can repeat a recipe to improve the weakest step, achieve a better final rating, or practice a troublesome gesture. Different recipes recombine familiar skills in new sequences.
games.kid_translation_note: A career activity could divide a real job into three or four safe, exaggerated gestures with clear demonstrations and visible results. Each step should be brief and forgiving while still rewarding careful timing.

games.title: The Oregon Trail
games.genre: Educational journey, resource-management, and risk simulation
games.target_player: Students and general players interested in historical journeys, planning, survival decisions, and emergent stories
games.goal: Lead a traveling party from Missouri to Oregon while managing supplies, health, time, weather, terrain, and unpredictable hazards.
games.core_action: Review party and resource status, choose purchases, pace, rations, routes, rests, river-crossing methods, and responses to events, then advance the journey and absorb the resulting costs or benefits.
games.information: The player reads distance, date, weather, terrain, party health, illnesses or injuries, food, ammunition, clothing, spare parts, money, wagon condition, landmark information, river depth and width, event messages, and advice available at stops.
constraints: Money at departure limits the initial supply mix.
Food, ammunition, clothing, medicine-related capacity, and wagon parts are finite.
Travel consumes food and calendar time.
Faster pace and lower rations can increase health risk.
Weather and seasons can make late arrival dangerous.
Wagon breakdowns require appropriate spare parts or costly delay.
River crossings force choices under incomplete risk information.
Random illness, injury, theft, loss, and death can undermine a sound plan.
decisions: How to allocate starting money across supplies
Which departure month balances preparation and seasonal risk
How fast to travel and how much food to ration
When to rest, trade, buy supplies, hunt, or continue
Which river-crossing method is worth its cost and risk
Whether a shortcut saves enough time to justify uncertainty
How to respond when several scarce resources are low at once
games.feedback: Status screens and event text report changing health, supplies, distance, date, breakdowns, illnesses, deaths, and environmental conditions. The wagon advances across a map, landmarks confirm progress, and the ending evaluates survival and remaining resources.
games.failure: Party members can die from illness, injury, starvation, exposure, accidents, or other hazards. The expedition can end when the entire party dies or can no longer continue; even a successful arrival may receive a weaker result if few people or supplies survive.
games.retry_motivation: A failed expedition creates a memorable causal story: too little food, a late departure, excessive pace, a dangerous crossing, or simple bad luck. Players retry to test a different supply plan, risk policy, route, or pacing strategy and see whether they can bring more people through.
games.mastery: Skilled players maintain reserves, understand the interaction between season, pace, rations, and health, avoid spending scarce resources on low-value choices, and select risks based on current recovery capacity rather than treating every event independently.
games.variation: Random weather, illness, accidents, river conditions, losses, hunting results, party composition, chosen occupation, starting purchases, routes, pace, and player risk tolerance create different expedition stories.
games.progression: The journey moves through landmarks and increasingly consequential resource pressure. Supplies decline, winter approaches, terrain changes, and accumulated injuries or equipment losses make later decisions depend on the quality of earlier planning.
games.reward: Distance traveled, landmark arrival, surviving party members, preserved supplies, successful risk management, final score, historical context, and the emergent story of the expedition reinforce play.
games.core_loop_statement: Inspect the expedition's condition, choose how much resource or risk to accept, advance toward the next landmark, and update the plan after events occur. The thinking lives in preserving enough flexibility for unknown future trouble while a seasonal deadline keeps the party moving.
games.mastery_statement: A novice optimizes the immediate problem or spends resources until a meter looks safe. An expert manages interacting reserves, thinks several landmarks ahead, and judges each risk by whether the party could recover from a bad outcome.
games.replay_statement: Another expedition can change the departure date, occupation, shopping list, pace, rationing, route, and crossing policy. Because events vary, the player can compare whether a strategy was robust or merely lucky.
games.kid_translation_note: A career journey could ask children to prepare a limited tool kit and guide a team through a workday containing uncertain requests. Keep consequences nonfatal and frame reserves, rest, and asking for help as responsible professional choices.

games.title: Two Point Hospital
games.target_player: Players who enjoy systems management, spatial planning, optimization, workplace simulation, and humorous problem-solving
games.goal: Design and operate hospitals that diagnose and cure patients while maintaining finances, staff performance, reputation, and scenario-specific objectives.
games.core_action: Observe patient flow and hospital statistics, build or modify rooms, hire and assign staff, adjust priorities and policies, then watch the simulation reveal queues, bottlenecks, costs, and treatment outcomes.
games.information: The player observes patient needs and paths, diagnosis progress, queues, room utilization, staff skills and traits, energy and morale, salary expectations, machine condition, cleanliness, temperature, attractiveness, finances, cure rate, reputation, emergencies, inspections, and scenario objectives.
constraints: Construction, equipment, salaries, training, and maintenance cost money.
Rooms require minimum sizes, doors, and particular equipment.
Only qualified staff can perform many specialized jobs.
Patients must move through diagnosis before appropriate treatment.
Walking distance and queues reduce throughput and patient survival chances.
Staff require breaks and can become tired, unhappy, or overworked.
Machines deteriorate and may require maintenance.
Building space and available plots limit layout.
Scenario star objectives require several performance targets at once.
decisions: Which rooms to build, where to place them, and when to duplicate them
Which applicants to hire and which skills to train
How to assign staff roles and break policies
Whether to prioritize diagnosis certainty, treatment speed, patient survival, or financial efficiency
When to expand into another building
How much to invest in room quality, machines, amenities, janitors, and support infrastructure
How to redesign the hospital when queues expose a bottleneck
games.feedback: Patients and staff visibly navigate the hospital, queues form outside rooms, machines operate or break, and humorous cures animate successful treatment. Pop-up messages, financial graphs, queue counts, cure rates, deaths, reputation, awards, inspections, emergencies, and objective meters quantify results.
games.failure: Poor management can cause long queues, low cure rates, deaths, unhappy staff, damaged reputation, and sustained financial losses. A hospital may become financially unsustainable, while individual scenario objectives can remain unmet until the player redesigns or improves operations.
games.retry_motivation: Bottlenecks are visible and invite targeted fixes such as another room, better routing, specialized training, or changed priorities. New layouts and staffing models can produce dramatic improvements, and higher scenario ratings reward continued optimization.
games.mastery: Skilled players design short patient routes, separate high-volume functions from specialist treatment, train focused staff, use job assignments deliberately, maintain spare capacity, and diagnose the actual system bottleneck before spending money.
games.variation: Patient arrivals, disease mix, staff applicant traits, emergencies, inspections, epidemics, maps, building shapes, climate conditions, objectives, layout choices, and staffing strategies vary hospital operation.
games.progression: Scenarios introduce new illnesses, diagnostic and treatment rooms, staff skills, environmental problems, and management objectives. One-, two-, and three-star targets demand increasingly strong performance, while unlocked tools support more complex hospitals.
games.reward: Treatment income, cure animations, expanding buildings, trained staff, improved statistics, higher reputation, awards, scenario stars, unlocked equipment and locations, and smoothly flowing patient traffic reinforce the loop.
games.core_loop_statement: Build a service system, watch workers and customers move through it, identify the next bottleneck, and spend limited resources to improve flow. The fun lives in discovering that layout, training, maintenance, and staffing interact, then seeing a redesigned workplace run smoothly.
games.mastery_statement: A novice reacts to the loudest queue by adding expensive rooms. An expert traces the whole service chain, distinguishes symptoms from root bottlenecks, specializes staff, and designs capacity and walking routes before demand peaks.
games.replay_statement: The same workplace problem can be addressed through a compact layout, extra capacity, better-trained staff, different diagnostic policies, or slower expansion. New maps and disease mixes test whether the player's management principles generalize.
games.kid_translation_note: A simplified career game could show customers moving through three workplace stations and let children place workers according to their skills. Visible queues make the effect of cooperation, layout, training, and rest understandable without exposing children to complex financial controls.

games.title: PowerWash Simulator
games.genre: First-person methodical cleaning and work simulation
games.target_player: Players who enjoy low-pressure tasks, visible completion, precise tool use, exploration of detailed objects, and relaxing audiovisual feedback
games.goal: Remove dirt from every required surface of each job site until the cleaning checklist reaches full completion.
games.core_action: Scan an object for remaining dirt, choose a washer configuration, aim and sweep the water stream across surfaces, reposition to reach hidden areas, and repeat until each component is marked clean.
games.information: The player observes dirty and clean surface contrast, a dirt-highlighting function, overall and component completion percentages, a list of object parts, cleaning completion notifications, surface distance and angle, washer strength, nozzle width, and the geometry of inaccessible areas.
constraints: Different washers and nozzles trade cleaning power for spray width or effective range.
Dirt may be hidden beneath, behind, above, or inside complex objects.
The water stream requires line of sight and an effective angle and distance.
Ladders, scaffolding, crouching, and repositioning are needed to reach some surfaces.
A component is not complete until nearly all of its required dirty area is removed.
Large jobs require sustained attention across many separately tracked parts.
decisions: Which section to clean first
Whether to use a narrow powerful stream or a wider faster sweep
Where to stand to expose the most surface area
When to clean methodically versus search specifically for missed spots
How to divide a large object into manageable zones
Whether a stubborn mark reflects insufficient power, poor angle, distance, or an overlooked surface
games.feedback: Dirt disappears exactly where the stream passes, revealing brighter colors and materials. Water sounds and visual spray accompany the action, component percentages rise, a distinctive notification marks each fully cleaned part, the checklist shrinks, payment is awarded, and a completion time-lapse summarizes the transformation.
games.failure: Standard jobs generally have little punitive failure. Inefficient technique mainly costs time and attention; the common obstacle is reaching a very high completion percentage while a tiny hidden patch remains. Progress is persistent enough that the player can continue searching rather than restart the job.
games.retry_motivation: The player is usually motivated to continue rather than retry because every cleaned patch remains as visible progress. Missed dirt becomes a contained search problem, while new jobs offer fresh shapes, transformations, tools, and opportunities for a more orderly technique.
games.mastery: Skilled players segment objects into zones, maintain consistent sweep spacing, select nozzles by dirt and geometry, work from angles that expose multiple surfaces, use the dirt highlight diagnostically, and consult component completion data to narrow the final search.
games.variation: Job size, object geometry, dirt coverage, surface materials, access angles, available equipment, optional cleaning order, and the player's chosen workflow vary the experience.
games.progression: Jobs grow from smaller objects to large, intricate environments containing many components and hidden surfaces. Earnings and career progress provide access to stronger washers, attachments, and equipment that improve reach or efficiency.
games.reward: Immediate clean streaks, revealed colors, component-completion notifications, rising percentages, money, equipment upgrades, finished-job transformations, checklist completion, and the final time-lapse reinforce the loop.
games.core_loop_statement: Choose a surface, sweep away visible dirt, inspect the result, and reposition or change tools for whatever remains. The pleasure comes from continuous before-and-after feedback, while the thinking lies in coverage patterns, tool choice, and locating the final hidden patches.
games.mastery_statement: A novice sprays wherever dirt is obvious and later searches a chaotic collection of missed spots. An expert cleans in deliberate zones, controls overlap and angle, and uses part-level information to finish with minimal backtracking.
games.replay_statement: A later job can be approached with a different cleaning order, nozzle strategy, route, or division into zones. Players can also try to produce a cleaner workflow with fewer missed patches and less repositioning.
games.kid_translation_note: A children's career game could turn tidying, inspecting, repairing, painting, or sorting into a persistent visible transformation with a checklist of small parts. A highlight button for remaining work preserves satisfaction while preventing the final search from becoming frustrating.
